newsitem.title: USA: Michigan says Ameritech meets most of checklist.
newsitem.headline: Michigan says Ameritech meets most of checklist.

text.p: Ameritech Corp. has met 11 of the 14 requirements of a federal checklist that must be satisfied before the Baby Bell can enter the $80 billion long-distance phone business, state regulators said Tuesday.

The Michigan Public Service Commission also said it believes Ameritech can meet the other three items before the Federal Communications Commission must decide whether to let the carrier offer long-distance service in Michigan.
"We believe that improvements in the three areas we have noted can be accomplished in the remaining 70 days prior to FCC action," Michigan commission Chairman John Strand said.
Ameritech said the findings support its application. But critics such as long-distance provider MCI Communications Corp. and others said the findings show why the FCC should reject Ameritech's bid.

Under last year's communications law, Ameritech and other regional Bells must satisfy a checklist showing they have opened their local phone monpolies to new competitors before they can offer long-distance service from their regions.
Chicago-based Ameritech was forced earlier this year to withdraw an initial application because of numerous errors.
State regulators and the U.S. Justice Department must provide the FCC with a recommendation.
"We're going to look at the three items that they're talking about and determine how to adderss them," an Ameritech spokeswoman said of the findings by Michigan regulators.
In the carrier's initial application, Michigan regulators had said Ameritech met the entire checklist.

MCI Communications attorney Jonathan Sallet argued the Michigan Public Service Commission "does not provide the same support it gave Ameritech in its previous fatally flawed application, which further demonstrates why this application must be denied."

Michigan regulators now say Ameritech must give other carriers better access to support services used to handle billing, repairs and new orders. They also cite problems with the sharing of facilities for handling phone traffic.
And they say Ameritech must improve the accuracy of its 911 emergency records.
Ameritech has pegged the long-distance market in its five-state region at $9 billion. It has said it hopes to offer the service in its five Midwestern states by the end of the year.
